claims.text: Cold-spray deposition of a high-performance alloy overlay can restore the damaged component.
Cold-spray repair avoids the hot-cracking defects typical of fusion-welding repair.
The repaired component will maintain its integrity under aggressive operating conditions.
The component substrate is predisposed to hot cracking and formation of an unfavorable heat-affected zone during fusion welding.
A cold-sprayed overlay bonds mechanically and possibly metallurgically to the substrate through high-velocity particle impact with minimal thermal input.
Cold-spray deposition preserves the original substrate microstructure and avoids formation of a deleterious heat-affected zone.
Cold spray avoids melting the repair material.
Avoiding melting prevents excessive thermal cycling that could trigger phase changes and hot cracking.
High-velocity deposition produces strong adhesion and may cause localized recrystallization at the repair interface.
Interfacial adhesion and localized recrystallization enable effective load transfer while maintaining microstructural stability.
The cold-spray-repaired component will have wear resistance and mechanical strength at least comparable to those of a fusion-weld-repaired component.
Cold-spray repair will significantly reduce hot-cracking incidence relative to fusion-welding repair.
Cold-spray repair will cause minimal microstructural degradation.
Traditional fusion welding introduces high heat input that causes hot cracking and an altered heat-affected zone, compromising repair integrity.
The cold-spray overlay can tolerate elevated-temperature wear conditions up to an unspecified interface-degradation limit.
The intervention is effective for components having limited accessible repair areas, provided operating temperature and stress remain below cold-spray bonding limits.
Cold-spray overlay repair may be unsuitable when the entire component volume must be rebuilt.
Extreme thermal cycling may deteriorate the cold-sprayed overlay bond.
